overview: The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy used Ravenna as a royal center. Its surviving buildings and personal ornaments show both distinctive traditions and close engagement with the Roman world.

items.text: Theodoric's mausoleum used large blocks of Istrian stone arranged around a central space.
Sant'Apollinare Nuovo began as Theodoric's palace chapel. Its mosaics combined Roman traditions with eastern Mediterranean influence.
The Arian Baptistery preserves imagery expressing the court's Christian faith. The Archbishop's Chapel represents a different Christian community in the same city.
In wider Ostrogothic dress, pairs of shoulder brooches secured women's long garments. Decorated belts, necklaces and other jewelry completed the ensemble.

A surviving brooch attributed to wider Ostrogothic material culture was cast in silver, with silver covering its copper-alloy pin. It combined practical fastening and ornament; the record does not establish manufacture in Italy.
Ravenna passed from Ostrogothic to Byzantine rule. Buildings surviving together today belong to different patrons and periods; San Vitale's Justinianic decoration should not be credited to Theodoric.
